The principles that once allowed the Assyrian state to exist therefore cannot serve today as stable foundations for every form of state.
Nor can the foundations of contemporary British politics necessarily serve the political life of future humanity.
This throws the whole idea of politically verifying a theory into question—including, in particular, the testimony given by states about the theories presented to them.
Something condemned as a dangerous lie by Assyrian censorship might today be recognized as true by British organs of propaganda, only to be condemned once again as false by the state of the future.
We will return at the end of this chapter to the related problems raised by this difficult question.
For now, however, one point must already be stressed.

If we accept the existence of history as an undeniable fact—that is, if we accept that human beings change fundamentally over time—we can avoid the complete scepticism that denies the possibility of knowledge about humanity only by appealing to the Hegelian-Marxist conception of world history as a kind of international tribunal.
We must assume that humanity “judges” during the course of its historical development in the same way that a state judges its citizens and the theories they put forward.
Only the theory recognized by humanity “at the end of time” can be regarded as definitively, absolutely true.
In other words, the true theory will be the one adopted by the final—absolute or ideal—state: the single state that will exist eternally and without further change.
Once again, then, we arrive at the conclusion that absolute knowledge of humanity can only be omniscience, verified by the integral state—that is, by communist society.
For the moment, however, our subject is not omniscience but philosophy: the path that leads toward it, or the true but partial knowledge that can be regarded as an embryo of universal truth.
Here we need to repeat the point once more: political verification makes the possibility of philosophical knowledge entirely secure.

First, there are theories about human beings that must be presupposed if we are to explain the possibility of any political life under any state at all. These theories can already be regarded as definitively true.
Second, we can identify theories that have been presupposed, either tacitly or explicitly, by every known state. These too can be regarded as true with a high degree of confidence.
And finally, even now we can sometimes decide between different theories that different states, at different times, have regarded as true or false.

At present, for example, the fact that England is not the property of the Assyrian state, whereas Mesopotamia is British property, means that, whatever other disagreements may remain, the knowledge contained in contemporary English political theory contains more truth than the knowledge embodied—tacitly or explicitly—in the political theory recognized by the Assyrian state.
Taking everything we have said together, then, we can maintain that technical and political verification establish, in principle, the possibility of attaining perfect knowledge.
And this also establishes the possibility of philosophy: of true knowledge that knows itself to be partial and imperfect, but understands itself as a constituent part of future omniscience.

We must stress once again, however, that if philosophy differs from wisdom only because its knowledge is partial, it is philosophy—that is, an aspiration toward wisdom and a path leading to it—only when it is fully aware of the partial character of its knowledge.
It must know how and why its knowledge is partial.
And it must explain how and why that knowledge can continue to expand without any fixed limit.

Philosophy must therefore know that it can enlarge its knowledge only by using the results supplied by the political and technical verification of human knowledge of the world—that is, knowledge of nature and history.
It must also understand that the very character of this verification makes its knowledge necessarily partial and therefore imperfect.
As long as technology has not become universal, philosophical knowledge is necessarily limited in space. Its knowledge of nature—its Cosmology—remains incomplete.

And as long as historical development continues, as long as the universal state has not been established, philosophical knowledge is necessarily limited in time. Its knowledge of the historical world—its Anthropology—remains incomplete.
As long as this remains the case, philosophy must “call into question” everything presented to it as “absolute truth,” including whatever philosophy itself may be tempted to regard in this way.
For philosophy knows that something declared true by the political tribunal of one particular historical moment may be declared false by the final judgment of the tribunal of world history.
Partial knowledge becomes philosophical knowledge, in other words, only when it contains, so to speak, the idea of omniscience within itself.
At that point it appears not only as philosophical knowledge but also as a philosophical problem.
Once philosophy becomes conscious of itself as partial knowledge striving toward universality, it necessarily understands itself as an attempt to turn every form of positive knowledge into a problem.
This brings us to the second aspect of philosophy.

Because philosophy exists as partial or fragmentary knowledge, it necessarily appears not simply—and ultimately not even mainly—as the art of giving the best possible answers to the greatest possible number of different questions.
It appears instead as the art of asking those questions in the best possible way.
That is the aspect of philosophy to which we must now turn.
2. Philosophy as the ability to ask questions

In one sense, philosophy properly begins at the place and moment when a proposition previously regarded as true is, for the first time, “called into question”—without being judged false because of any internal contradiction or because it conflicts with evidence supplied by experimental verification, whether technical or political.
The same applies when a proposition previously regarded as false is reopened and therefore placed in question, even though no new reason has appeared for considering it true.
In other words, what characterizes philosophy is doubt about the truth or falsity of claims that have been asserted or rejected.

Any proposition therefore becomes philosophical, in a sense, as soon as we stop treating it as a truth or error settled once and for all and begin treating it instead as the subject of an investigation.
In this respect, philosophy is diametrically opposed to mythmaking: to the natural human tendency to regard every claim we make ourselves, or hear from someone else, as either true or false.

Philosophy is precisely the human capacity to refrain from treating any proposition as simply true or false, and instead to investigate it while “suspending judgment”—or, if you prefer, the capacity to “doubt” any assertion whatsoever.
But this philosophy, which stands opposed to mythmaking, must not be confused with sceptical philosophy.
Scepticism denies that human beings can genuinely distinguish truth from falsehood and therefore treats the “suspension of judgment” as the one attitude that must be maintained permanently.
Philosophy, by contrast, regards the suspension of judgment as only a temporary necessity.
Its doubt is not an end in itself. It is simply a means of establishing the truth once and for all.
We might say that the philosopher aspires to the same “absolute” truth as the maker of myths.

Both seek a form of discourse that is genuinely “convincing”: one that could be accepted definitively and irrevocably by everyone who understands it, because its meaning corresponds perfectly to an objective content that exists independently of that discourse and is nevertheless expressed by it.

But unlike the mythmaker, the philosopher knows that a discourse which persuades me personally—which produces subjective conviction—is not therefore objectively true. My conviction cannot serve as a guarantee of its truth.
Like the sceptic, the philosopher knows that the same person can change their convictions and that different people can hold radically different convictions.
But the philosopher does not draw the sceptical conclusion that truth and true knowledge are therefore inaccessible.
Instead, he looks for the means by which such knowledge can be reached.
So when philosophy calls for a “suspension of judgment,” it does so only until absolute knowledge has been attained.
For philosophy, then—at least at the beginning—any proposition is neither true nor false but open to doubt.
It is neither an affirmation nor a negation.

This purely philosophical impulse—the art of turning any claim presented as true or false into a problem, a question, and a subject for investigation—first emerged openly and consciously in ancient Greece. People who possessed this art gradually came to be known as “sophists.” Most of the sophists, however, used it in a sceptical and destructive way. There was only one of them—Socrates—whose activity could properly be called philosophy. And since we know Socrates’ philosophical activity almost entirely through the “Socratic” dialogues of his great pupil Plato, Plato can reasonably be regarded as the father of philosophical questioning.

Unlike the sophists, Plato’s Socrates did not ask questions in order to “confound” someone—to leave him permanently unable to answer and therefore unable to distinguish truth from falsehood. He asked them in order to give people grounds for hoping that every possible question might eventually have an answer. In other words, Plato’s Socrates strives for wisdom, and is therefore a philosopher in the true sense. But he assumes that the philosopher can reach this goal, or at least approach it, only by learning how to ask questions—by mastering the art of turning into a question everything that he himself or anyone else is inclined to accept immediately, without prior investigation, as either true or false. Plato called this philosophy of questioning and doubt—this attempt to approach objective truth through the critical examination of subjective “truth”—dialectic.

For Plato, philosophy in the broad sense therefore has two basic parts. There is, first, the art of asking questions and, second, the art of answering them. Or, in Plato’s own terms, philosophy divides into dialectic and dogmatics. Dialectic is nothing other than philo-sophy in the strict sense: the pursuit of final knowledge and the path that leads toward it. Dogmatics, by contrast, is in principle no longer “philo-sophy” but sophia itself—wisdom, understood as perfect knowledge or omniscience. Yet because Plato regarded wisdom as unattainable for human beings, at least during earthly life, his dogmatics also remained philosophical in character. It was knowledge, but only partial knowledge, and therefore neither final nor absolutely true. Even so, there remains an essential difference between dogmatics and dialectic, both in their aims and in the methods they use. The philosopher may know that his “dogmatics” remains, in the end, questionable or problematic. Nevertheless, he must present it as the partial knowledge that should for the time being be regarded as true—at least until it is replaced by something closer to absolute or final truth. Dialectic, by contrast, does not claim to be knowledge itself. It claims only to be the path toward knowledge. It neither denies nor affirms anything; it only asks questions. It does not give answers, but prepares the ground on which a “dogmatic” answer can eventually be given.

Since we have already discussed philosophy as partial knowledge, we will not examine Plato’s dogmatics here. What we now need to consider is what Plato means by the dialectical or questioning part of philosophy—or, if one prefers, its dialectical and interrogative aspect.

Plato’s Socrates begins from the same point as scepticism in developing his idea of dialectic. He starts from the fact that there are many “myths” or theses that claim to be true and that may each be subjectively convincing, even though they are mutually incompatible. Their obvious incompatibility proves that they cannot all be true. Yet because they may all seem equally convincing, there is no immediate way to distinguish the true ones from the false ones. Each of them may therefore be true or false, without our yet being able to know which it is.

Plato called such theses opinions—doxa—and opposed them to true knowledge—epistēmē. The first task of philosophy is therefore to learn, and to teach others, how to distinguish knowledge from opinion. Knowledge can be accepted as a “dogma,” meaning a final and unchanging truth. An opinion, by contrast, must be turned into an impartial question, regardless of whether it originally appeared as an affirmation or a denial. In other words, it must become the subject of critical investigation. The result of that investigation will either be that the opinion is rejected as false—in which case it was an error—or that it survives as an unquestionable truth and thereby becomes knowledge. This is the basic task of dialectic.

Platonic dialectic must therefore teach us to treat as mere opinion—and thus to question—anything that claims to be knowledge without sufficient grounds. To do this, one must show that a proposition opposed to the supposed knowledge can be just as convincing as the original proposition itself. This happens spontaneously when two opposing forms of “knowledge” collide in a discussion. If neither can prove its claim to truth, both are exposed as mere opinions. Together they then form a question waiting for an answer: a subject for investigation. This is why discussion, or dialogue, becomes the fundamental instrument of dialectic—and, indeed, explains its name.

In this sense, dialectic has existed for as long as human speech itself. We encounter it constantly in everyday life whenever firm assertions turn into open questions. We have already seen this kind of dialectical transformation ourselves when we discussed the passage from naïve rationalism to scepticism. Socrates therefore did not “invent” dialectic. He merely became conscious of it. He learned to do systematically what had previously happened by accident, involuntarily, and without awareness. And he did so because he was consciously trying to reach the truth by this means.

There is no guarantee, however, that a person who makes some judgement will ever meet anyone who challenges it. He may never encounter an opponent who advances the contrary view or shows him that this contrary view is at least as “convincing” as his own. And even if he does meet such an opponent, he may simply fail to find the opposing argument convincing. So long as he does not actively seek out opposition, he may go through his entire life without ever noticing that what he takes to be “knowledge” is nothing more than an untested opinion.

Socrates created his “dialectical method” to help people avoid this kind of self-deception. When someone expresses an opinion, Socrates does not simply oppose it with a contrary judgement of his own and present that judgement as the truth. Instead, by means of leading questions, he makes the person himself “change his mind” and eventually defend the opposite of what he originally claimed. Since it is the same person who has now advanced two contradictory views, he can no longer avoid regarding them as equally “convincing.” Yet because they contradict each other, he cannot regard them both as true. If he refuses to choose arbitrarily between them, he must begin to see both as mere “opinions.” His supposed knowledge thereby becomes a problem for which he must seek a solution.

In other words, once Socrates has subjected someone to this “dialectical treatment,” that person himself becomes what we call a dialectician: a philosopher who is no longer satisfied with mere opinion but strives for knowledge.

But the dialectic of Plato’s Socrates is not needed only to turn a non-philosopher into a philosopher. It is equally indispensable to philosophers themselves. Dialectic is not merely an introduction to philosophy. It is philosophy itself—or, more precisely, its first and non-dogmatic part. To discover genuine knowledge, the philosopher must be able to distinguish it from everything that remains merely opinion. And he can do this only by subjecting opinion to dialectical treatment—that is, by means of dialogue or discussion.

Socrates claimed that he differed from other people only in one respect: he knew that he knew nothing. Yet he acquired this dialectical “knowledge” of his ignorance precisely through the discussions and dialogues in which he demonstrated to his opponents that what they called “knowledge” was, in the end, merely opinion.

From the standpoint of Plato’s Socrates, then, a human being who withdraws from society and isolates himself can possess nothing but “opinions.” Some of these opinions may happen to be true—ortho-dox—but the person who holds them will never know that they are. He will not even know how to distinguish knowledge from opinion and will therefore automatically mistake opinion for knowledge.

In other words, an isolated person can never become either a philosopher or, a fortiori, a sage. He can become one only by way of dialectic: through discussion, dialogue, or, more generally, through participation in society by means of speech.

So far, however, we have seen only that dialectic can reveal that something which takes itself to be knowledge is really only an opinion. We have seen that dialectic can turn any affirmation or denial into a question. But how can it help us find answers to the questions it produces? How can genuine and final knowledge be built out of mere opinions once we have clearly recognized them as opinions?

According to Plato’s Socrates, the answer lies in the very principle that is always more or less consciously acknowledged by people who take part in “discussion,” “debate,” “dispute,” “controversial conferences,” as well as in “reviews,” “critical reviews,” “polemical articles,” and everything else written and published for similar purposes. In all these activities, it is assumed—usually silently and without much reflection—that truth emerges from the confrontation between differing, mutually exclusive opinions. In dialogues, disputes, discussions, and so on, opposing opinions destroy one another, and on the ruins of that mutual destruction only true knowledge remains.
Using the terminology introduced by Hegel and later popularized by Marx, we can picture the dialectical process as follows.

For naïve, non-dialectical, myth-making thought, every opinion that is internally coherent, consistent with experience, and not disproved by technical or political experimentation automatically appears as the one and only truth—the final truth, or a “dogma.”

For dialectic, however, such a dogma is only a thesis, and every thesis necessarily gives rise to a directly opposed opinion: an antithesis. As they stand, both thesis and antithesis are merely opinions.
The first task of dialectic is therefore to turn every supposed piece of knowledge into a “thesis” or an “opinion” by finding the corresponding antithesis.

Its second task is to bring thesis and antithesis into interaction. They must be investigated, first of all by comparing and confronting them. The thesis must be examined from the standpoint of the antithesis, and the antithesis from the standpoint of the thesis.

Through this interaction, thesis and antithesis, which at first confront each other mechanically as opposites, enter into something like a chemical combination and form a new whole called a synthesis.

Within this synthesis, thesis and antithesis lose everything that was one-sided in them—precisely those features that made them incompatible. And it was their one-sidedness that originally made them a “pair”: because each was one-sided, each claimed to represent knowledge in its entirety. Once their one-sidedness is overcome through dialectical discussion, they become compatible and together form the complete knowledge contained in the synthesis. The synthesis is therefore no longer merely an opinion to which some other opinion can be opposed. It is a single body of knowledge.

Of course, this is not reached immediately. The first synthesis may itself turn out to be only a new thesis, which necessarily generates a new antithesis; together they then produce a new synthesis, and so on. Ultimately, however, the dialectical process must arrive at a form of knowledge that can no longer be subjected to dialectical treatment. This knowledge then constitutes the second part of philosophy: dogmatism.

To sum up: from Plato’s standpoint, the isolated individual never reaches knowledge and is condemned to remain forever within the realm of opinion. But human beings are not alone. They do not merely monologue; they also engage in dialogue. And through dialogue a person can discover that what he took for knowledge was only an opinion. Once he sees this, he can begin to strive for knowledge—that is, he can become a philosopher.

Philosophy therefore necessarily presupposes social interaction between human beings. Truth, and ultimately wisdom, will either never be discovered at all or will be discovered precisely through this interaction.

Yet this interaction is not action in the proper sense. It is neither work nor struggle. It is only a logical contact between human beings, a contact that takes place through speech. If monologue is not enough to discover truth, dialogue nevertheless would be.

This passive and non-active understanding of dialectic—as something that belongs purely to discourse and logic—survived until Hegel. But although classical philosophy preserved the defect of Platonic dialectic, it gradually forgot its positive feature: its social character.

Philosophers ceased to realize that the pursuit of knowledge and truth has no chance of success, and indeed no meaning, outside society and communication with other people. They began to believe that a philosopher could attain wisdom in complete solitude, “conversing” only with himself.

Once philosophy had forgotten—or failed to understand—the social character of Platonic dialectic, even though this social character is the beating heart of philosophy and the very basis of its existence, it had little choice but gradually to abandon dialectic itself. “Dogmatics” ceased to be the second part of philosophy, arising as the result of its first, dialectical part. Instead, dogmatics became philosophy as such. And once dogmatic philosophy stopped discussing human opinions dialectically, it began to seek knowledge through the immediate and solitary contemplation of a reality beyond the human world.
The dialectical part of philosophy was never completely abandoned, however. It merely became accidental, involuntary, and unconscious.

Aristotle, although he still wrote dialogues, no longer gave dialectic the place Plato had given it. Yet even in his “dogmatic” works he retained a dialectical moment under the name of aporia. Before offering a solution to any problem, he first turned it into a question and listed different possible propositions as contradictory solutions—the aporias. And quite often he stopped there, without going beyond the stage of questioning.

These “aporias” then passed into the scholastic tradition, where entire treatises were written according to the principle of Sic et Non—“Yes and No”—most famously by Abelard. Every thesis was opposed by an antithesis, although no real solution was necessarily provided, or at least no solution beyond a more or less tolerable synthesis of the contradictions.

More generally, the critical and polemical sections of philosophical writings came in practice to take the place of philosophy’s dialectical part. The same can be said of the history of philo-sophy itself, which has long been regarded as an indispensable part of philosophical education.

In all these cases, however, dialectic is merely incidental. It is not regarded as necessary. In principle, it is assumed that the philosopher could dispense with it and reach truth and knowledge without having to confront error and opinion along the way.
At the beginning of modern philosophy, however, dialectic reappears in Descartes as a necessary first part of philosophy.

Descartes once again understood that what a person immediately forms is only an opinion, which he then naturally mistakes for knowledge. To reach genuine knowledge, one must first become convinced of this fact—which means doubting everything and turning everything into a question.

Descartes tells us that he himself reached his dogmatic philosophy through a systematic discipline of scepticism. He also shows that it is impossible to become a philosopher without passing through this discipline.
And it is easy to see that his scepticism is strongly dialectical, because he calls into question everything that can be doubted—that is, every assertion that is no more convincing than its opposite.

But Descartes does not yet possess the idea of dialectical synthesis. He rejects thesis and antithesis alike, keeping as knowledge only those assertions for which no antithetical reversal is possible. In practice, what remains is the claim that the I and the divine being exist. Descartes then believes it possible to derive, or “deduce,” from these claims all the knowledge that remains accessible to human beings.

Clearly, this is an illusion. But it is worth noticing that Descartes once again makes dialectic a necessary and introductory part of philosophy. He does so because he believes that knowledge can be distinguished from opinion only after it has undergone dialectical treatment—that is, only after it has first been returned to the state of a question by establishing the possibility of an opposing opinion.
Yet Descartes completely rejects the social side of dialectic. He assumes that this entire dialectical transformation can take place within a solitary Meditation.

A human being can reach truth not only without doing anything, but even without entering into dialogue. It is enough for him to meditate—and perhaps, afterward, to tell his friends what he has discovered. Indeed, without society he might not even have opinions in the first place. He could therefore reach knowledge without passing through any social interaction at all.
